reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Urea cycle disorder caused by biallelic CPS1 variants affecting the first, rate-limiting mitochondrial step of ureagenesis
Severe neonatal form presents with rapidly progressive hyperammonaemic encephalopathy: poor feeding, vomiting, tachypnoea, hypotonia, seizures and coma
Biochemistry shows marked hyperammonaemia with low/normal citrulline, low arginine, raised glutamine and characteristically low urine orotic acid
Low orotic aciduria distinguishes it (and NAGS deficiency) from ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, in which orotic acid is high
Milder, later-onset presentations feature episodic hyperammonaemia, protein intolerance and neurocognitive problems
Biochemically indistinguishable from NAGS deficiency, so a carglumic acid trial and gene testing are used to separate the two
Confirm with CPS1 sequencing; enzyme assay requires liver tissue and is now rarely needed
Acute management is emergency ammonia removal (haemodialysis/haemofiltration if severe), nitrogen scavengers, arginine and protein restriction; liver transplantation is definitive for severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 is the mitochondrial enzyme that initiates the urea cycle by condensing ammonia and bicarbonate into carbamoyl phosphate, a reaction that absolutely requires N-acetylglutamate as an allosteric activator. When CPS1 activity is deficient, waste nitrogen cannot enter the urea cycle, so ammonia accumulates to toxic levels while downstream urea cycle intermediates (citrulline, arginine) are low. Because carbamoyl phosphate is not overproduced, it is not shunted into the pyrimidine pathway, so orotic acid excretion remains low, a key feature shared with NAGS deficiency and distinguishing both from the more distal OTC deficiency. Hyperammonaemia is directly neurotoxic, causing cerebral oedema and encephalopathy, particularly in the neonate. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency (near-identical biochemistry, carglumic acid responsive)
Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency (raised orotic acid, X-linked)
Fatty acid oxidation disorders with hyperammonaemia
additionalInvestigations: Urgent plasma ammonia during suspected crises
Plasma amino acids (low citrulline and arginine, raised glutamine)
Blood gas showing respiratory alkalosis with hyperammonaemia
Carglumic acid trial to help distinguish from NAGS deficiency
Plasma acylcarnitines/organic acids to exclude secondary hyperammonaemia
redFlags: Neonatal hyperammonaemic coma requiring emergency dialysis
Cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure from severe hyperammonaemia
Rapidly rising ammonia with deteriorating consciousness at any age
Decompensation during catabolic illness, high protein intake or surgery
Failure of ammonia to fall despite scavenger and dietary measures
reference.prognosis: The severe neonatal form carries a high risk of death or permanent neurological disability related to the depth and duration of hyperammonaemia, whereas milder late-onset disease can be managed medically; liver transplantation corrects the hepatic enzyme defect and can prevent further crises.
pitfalls: Delaying ammonia measurement and dialysis in an encephalopathic neonate
Confusing CPS1 with OTC deficiency by not checking orotic acid
Not separating CPS1 from NAGS deficiency, missing the carglumic-acid-responsive disorder
Under-dialysing when ammonia is dangerously high and scavengers alone are inadequate
Failing to establish an emergency regimen and long-term dietary/scavenger plan
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
Saudubray, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Emergency management of hyperammonaemic crisis by stopping protein intake and giving high-calorie glucose (with intralipid) to reverse catabolism
Nitrogen-scavenging therapy with sodium benzoate and sodium phenylbutyrate to provide alternative routes of nitrogen excretion
Arginine or citrulline supplementation to replenish depleted urea cycle intermediates
Haemodialysis or haemofiltration for severe or refractory hyperammonaemia to clear ammonia rapidly
Long-term protein-restricted diet with essential amino acid supplementation supervised by a metabolic dietitian
A carglumic acid trial to distinguish from and treat NAGS deficiency
Liver transplantation for definitive correction of the hepatic enzyme defect and prevention of further crises
Genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal recessive inheritance, with regular monitoring of plasma ammonia and amino acids
